subject: Why does boxplot require both x and y "dimensions"?

messages.author: afa289b81aad98c2
messages.subject: Why does boxplot require both x and y "dimensions"?
parts:
Hi all... I'm teaching a chemometrics, course, and have taught the
students to use qplot for all their work, which has worked out very
well. In the process however, they have observed some things which I
cannot explain to them. To wit:

data(diamonds)
qplot(x = carat, data = diamonds, geom = "histogram") # works fine, as
does "density"

but

qplot(x = carat, data = diamonds, geom = "boxplot")

doesn't work, it wants a y value. I can't explain why this is to
students because to me, boxplot is a way of displaying univariate
statistics, as is histogram or density. Further, the documentation
seems to say that only x is required:

The following aesthetics can be used with geom_boxplot. Aesthetics are
mapped to variables in the data with the aes function:
geom_boxplot(aes(x = var))

Of course one can give boxplot a legitimate set of x and y values, or
even a dummy of sorts:

qplot(x = 1, y = carat, data = diamonds, geom = "boxplot")

So, how do I explain this? My best answer to date is that histogram
or density compute their own y values, but boxplot doesn't have any
corresponding value - the width of the boxplot along the x direction
is arbitrary or set for good looks, not information. Sounds OK, but
seems to be a little off from the documentation.

By the way, geom = "point" requires both x and y be specified, even if
the data is univariate. I guess the issue in laying out the plot is
the same as with boxplot. But this is a little easier to explain (or
at least I came to the answer faster) because "point" is designed for
bivariate plotting, so plotting only univariate data is a bit of a
special case.

OK, I think I have answered by own question, but if any one has a
better way to explain it, or if I'm dead-wrong, let me know!

Thanks, Bryan

messages.subject: Re: Why does boxplot require both x and y "dimensions"?
parts:
Boxplots are not just for univariate data. One of their major uses is
to compare the distribution of a continuous variable across different
levels of a categorical variable, in which case the categorical
variable is mapped to the x position.

An example using Fisher's cat data from the MASS library (included
with R):

require(MASS)
qplot(Sex,Bwt,data=cats,geom='boxplot')

> seems to be a little off from the documentation.

Technically, the required aesthetics for geom_boxplot are x, lower,
upper, middle, ymin and ymax, but most of the time you don't supply
these yourself, but they are calculated from stat_boxplot. In turn,
stat_boxplot just requires x and y (and I apologise if this isn't
clear from the documentation).

Your definition of a boxplot requiring only x values is perfectly
valid, but I chose to require both x and y because in most situations
you are using multiple boxplots (and I'd argue that if you're not, you
should be using a histogram instead). So there are multiple valid
(but conflicting) definitions, and I've just chosen the one that in my
experience is used most commonly.
